Vs.

full_judgment: 16. On perusal of the evidence of PW-17, the Magistrate, it appears that he categorically narrated the sequences as to how he recorded the confessional statement of Haris. In his cross examination he stated that the confessing accused was produced at 12.00 O'clock in his chamber by the police. Thereafter upon complying with all the formalities the confessional statement was recorded by him. He categorically denied the suggestion by the defence that he did not comply with the official formalities and filled up the form in accordance with law or that the confessing accused was not asked about the torture by the police. On perusal of the confessional statement (Ext-5) it appears that the learned Magistrate categorically stated therein that the confessing accused was not forced or compelled to make such statement by the police before making such confession nor there was any mark of injury on the person of the confessing accused nor the confessing accused told him about any torture or threat by the police. One more thing is to be mentioned that there is no prayer for retracting from the statement by the confessing accused. So the confessional statement appears to be voluntary though the defence took a plea that it was obtained by threat and torture. If the confessional statement appears to have been made voluntarily and found to be true, as has been found by the trial court the same can be accepted as an evidence. It is true that the statement made under section 164 of the Code can never be the basis of convicting the accused as the same cannot be used against any persons other than the person making it and unless the same is voluntary, true in nature and unless the same is corroborated by any other independent witness. Since the prosecution has been able to prove by PW-17 the Magistrate, that the confession was voluntary and taken in accordance with law the presumption of truthfulness of such statement, is available under section 80 of the Evidence Act and there is conclusiveness of the effect of such admission under section 31. Admission is the best evidence that the opponent can rely upon and though not conclusive for decisive of the matter unless successfully withdrawn or proved to be erroneous as has been decided in the case of Narayan Vs. Gopal reported in AIR 1960 SC 100. It can be shown to be erroneous or untrue, so long as the persons to whom it was made has not acted upon it to his detriment, when it might become conclusive by way of estoppel as has been decided in the case of Avadhikishor Vs. Ram reported in AIR 1979(SC)861.
